common_name: Grand Soleil d'Or Daffodil (Warm-Climate Yellow-and-Orange Tazetta)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; a classic warm-climate tazetta long grown as a cut flower on the French Riviera and one of the best-adapted daffodils for the low-chill Gulf South.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Grand Soleil d'Or produces clusters of small, intensely fragrant flowers with golden-yellow petals surrounding a deeper orange cup, several blooms per stem in the tazetta group's characteristic multi-flowered fashion. Bred for essentially chill-free climates, it perennializes reliably in the Gulf South where many trumpet and large-cup daffodil cultivars fail to return after the first year for lack of a proper winter chill. Allow the foliage to die back naturally after bloom without braiding or cutting it, since it recharges the bulb for next year's flowers, and leave established clumps undisturbed to naturalize and multiply over time.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Bulbs for Texas

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; a fragrant jonquilla hybrid noted as a reliable perennializer in the low-chill winters of the South.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Falconet bears clusters of three to four small, fragrant flowers per stem, golden-yellow petals surrounding a contrasting orange-red cup, on a plant that reliably returns and multiplies year after year in Southern gardens where many Northern-bred daffodil cultivars fail to perennialize due to insufficient winter chill. Its jonquil parentage gives it narrow, rush-like foliage and good heat tolerance once established. Allow the foliage to die back naturally after bloom without braiding or cutting it, since it recharges the bulb for next year's flowers, and leave established clumps undisturbed to naturalize over time.

common_name: Hawera Daffodil (Miniature Nodding Pale Yellow Triandrus Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; a miniature triandrus daffodil bearing multiple nodding, reflexed flowers per stem.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Hawera bears three to five small, pale lemon-yellow flowers per stem with distinctly swept-back, reflexed petals typical of the triandrus group, nodding gracefully on thin wiry stems above narrow, grassy foliage. Its diminutive scale and dainty, multi-flowered habit make it a good choice for a rock garden, the front of a bulb border, or naturalizing in short turf grass. Like other triandrus types it prefers a somewhat cooler climate than the heat-adapted tazetta and jonquilla types, so gardeners in the hottest parts of the Gulf South may find it a shorter-lived perennial than heirloom Southern daffodils. Allow the foliage to die back naturally after bloom without braiding or cutting it, since it recharges the bulb for next year's flowers.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Yellow Cheerfulness bears clusters of fully double, richly fragrant flowers in soft creamy yellow, several to a stem in the tazetta group's characteristic multi-flowered fashion, a warm-toned sport of the classic white double heirloom Cheerfulness. Its late-season bloom extends the daffodil display after most single-flowered cultivars have finished, and its tazetta parentage gives it good perennializing performance in the low-chill winters of the South. Allow the foliage to die back naturally after bloom without braiding or cutting it, since it recharges the bulb for next year's flowers, and leave established clumps undisturbed to naturalize over time.

common_name: Chinese Sacred Lily Daffodil (Heirloom Bunch-Flowered Tazetta for Forcing and Garden)
scientific_name: Narcissus tazetta var. orientalis 'Chinese Sacred Lily'

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, or force in a shallow bowl of pebbles and water indoors over winter for fragrant bloom; a historic tazetta long passed down in Southern gardens and traditionally associated with the Lunar New Year.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in fall, or set bulbs in a shallow bowl of pebbles and water indoors in late fall for fragrant winter bloom without any soil at all. Chinese Sacred Lily bears clusters of intensely fragrant flowers with white petals surrounding a golden-yellow cup, several blooms per stem in classic tazetta fashion, a heirloom form long grown both as a Southern garden perennial and, when forced in water, as a traditional Lunar New Year bloom in Chinese households. As a warm-climate tazetta it perennializes reliably in the Gulf South where many trumpet and large-cup daffodil cultivars fail for lack of winter chill. Garden-planted bulbs should have their foliage allowed to die back naturally after bloom without braiding or cutting it, since it recharges the bulb for next year's flowers.
